title: Pat Murphy’s Misstep May Have Cost Brewers a World Series Spot, OutKick Reports
body:
Milwaukee’s postseason fortunes took a dramatic turn in the bottom of the ninth inning of Game 4, when manager Pat Murphy elected to bring reliever Shane Drohan to the mound instead of the hot‑handed rookie Jacob Misiorowski. The decision backfired as the Brewers surrendered the lead, allowing the opposing team to tie the game and ultimately force a decisive extra‑innings showdown that could determine the outcome of the World Series.

The move sparked immediate controversy among analysts and fans alike because Misiorowski had been dominant throughout the playoffs, posting a sub‑2.00 ERA and striking out more than a batter per inning. Drohan, while experienced, had struggled in high‑leverage situations earlier in the season, posting a 4.87 ERA over his last 20 appearances. Murphy’s choice appeared to be rooted in conventional wisdom—favoring a veteran arm in a pressure‑filled moment—but the result underscored the growing debate over how far teams should rely on traditional bullpen hierarchies versus data‑driven matchups.

Milwaukee entered the series riding an eight‑game winning streak that had carried them past the San Diego Padres, Los Angeles Dodgers and Tampa Bay Rays, a run that seemed to cement their status as the league’s most resilient club. The Brewers’ offense had been firing on all cylinders, and their bullpen had been a cornerstone of the run, delivering clutch outs in multiple elimination games. Yet the Game 4 miscue highlighted a vulnerability that opponents have been probing all season: the thin margin between confidence in a veteran and the raw talent of a breakout rookie.

Baseball strategists note that Murphy’s decision reflects a broader trend in the sport where managers must balance the intangible “big‑game” experience with the cold, hard numbers that modern analytics provide. In the past decade, teams that have embraced advanced metrics in bullpen usage—such as the Tampa Bay Rays and Houston Astros—have often gained a strategic edge in the postseason. By opting for Drohan, Murphy may have inadvertently signaled a reluctance to fully trust the analytics that have propelled Misiorowski’s rise, a hesitation that could have ramifications beyond this single game.

The fallout from the decision was immediate. The Brewers’ bullpen, which had been a source of confidence, now faced scrutiny, and the clubhouse atmosphere grew tense as players and coaches reassessed their approach. Opponents, sensing the shift in momentum, capitalized on the opening, extending the game and forcing the Brewers into a grueling extra‑innings marathon that tested both stamina and composure. While Milwaukee ultimately managed to pull ahead in the 12th inning, the narrow escape left a lingering question: could a different choice have secured a more comfortable victory and preserved the team’s momentum heading into a potential Game 5?

Looking ahead, the Brewers must quickly reconcile the strategic misstep and reestablish trust in their decision‑making process. With the series now tied, Pat Murphy faces pressure to demonstrate adaptability, possibly integrating more data‑driven insights into his bullpen management while still respecting the veteran presence that has long defined his coaching philosophy. For Milwaukee’s fan base, the episode serves as a reminder that even the most successful runs can be derailed by a single tactical choice. As the World Series progresses, the Brewers’ ability to learn from this lapse and adjust on the fly could prove decisive in their quest to capture the championship.
